A.explanation: Dividing $6.40 \times 10^{-20} \text{ C}$ by $e$ gives $0.4e$, which is not an integer multiple of the elementary charge.

B.explanation: Dividing $4.00 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ by $e$ gives $2.5e$, which is not a whole number of elementary charges.

C.explanation: Dividing $1.12 \times 10^{-18} \text{ C}$ by $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ gives $7$, so it equals $7e$ and is quantised.

D.explanation: Dividing $9.11 \times 10^{-18} \text{ C}$ by $e$ gives about $56.9$, which is not an integer number of elementary charges.

hints: Notice the four values are all of order $10^{-20}$ to $10^{-18} \text{ C}$, so compare each to the elementary charge $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.
Recall charge is quantised: any isolated particle must carry $Q = ne$ where $n$ is a positive or negative integer.
Divide each listed charge by $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ and look for the one that gives a whole-number result with no remainder.
walkthrough: Identify the quantisation rule: possible charge $Q = ne$, with $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ and $n = 1, 2, 3...$.
For each option calculate $n = Q/e$ to test if it is an integer.
For $1.12 \times 10^{-18} \text{ C}$, write $Q = 11.2 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ to simplify division.
The other values give $0.4$, $2.5$ and about $56.9$, which are non-integers and so cannot occur as net charge.
An integer $n = 7$ means the charge is $7$ elementary charges, which is allowed. This is option C.
